title: Dig within
hookLine: within is the fountain of good, and it bubbles up if you keep digging (Meditations 7.59)
last: THE SAME YOU, WITH THE SAME TOOLS.

cards: When you're running on empty, where do you go? A lot of people go out. Another coffee.
A pep talk video. A friend who'll tell us we're doing great. A new book promising the secret.
None of that is bad. But it's like carrying water in cups from someone else's tap. It runs out, and you're back at the door.
A new week starts today. It's called cooked, and it's about what happens to us under heat. But first, Marcus points somewhere we forget to look for water.

teach.h: WITHIN IS THE FOUNTAIN OF GOOD.
teach.b: Book Seven, section fifty-nine, in George Long's translation: "Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig."

teach.h: A WELL IN A DRY COUNTRY.
teach.b: Picture a well in a dry country. The water is there, underground, but you won't see it from the surface. You have to dig, and once you reach it, you keep the well clear, or the sand fills it in again.
For Marcus the fountain is the part of you that can reason, choose and do good. The Stoics believed every human being carries a spark of the same reason that orders the universe.
So the good isn't something you have to buy, borrow or earn from outside. It's already down there. Notice two small words in the line: ever, twice.

teach.h: EVER BUBBLE UP, IF YOU EVER DIG.
teach.b: It will ever bubble up, if you will ever dig. It's a promise with a condition. The spring doesn't run dry, but the digging never finishes.
You don't dig once and live off it forever. You dig this morning, and again tonight. Many traditions share a picture like this.
Jesus speaks of a spring of water welling up inside. The Upanishads talk of the self hidden in the heart. Let each keep its own meaning.
For Marcus, it's plain and practical: when you need patience, courage or kindness, don't only look for someone to hand it to you. Your line: look down, too.

how: Readers of Marcus often treat this line as a call to daily reflection, a few minutes of looking inward each morning or evening, as Marcus himself seems to have done in writing his notes.

o: keep searching inside for the good already there
turn away from people and look only at yourself

games.why: look within, he writes: the good is there, and it bubbles up as long as you keep digging.

practice: Let your attention go down, below the noise of the day, the way a bucket goes down a well, and ask quietly: what's good in me right now?
Patience, a little warmth, a steadiness, even just being awake; don't force it, just keep digging gently, breath by breath. If you'd like a third minute, keep going.
